[[basketball]] executive and former professional player. He played for the [[Shanghai Sharks]] of the [[Chinese Basketball Association]] (CBA), and then spent his entire nine-year [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA) career with the [[Houston Rockets]]. He was an eight-time [[NBA All-Star]], and was named to the [[All-NBA Team]] five times. At {{convert|7|ft|6|in}}, he was the NBA's [[List of tallest players in NBA history|tallest active player]] in his final season.{{cite web |url=http://www.nba.com/playerfile/yao_ming/index.html |title=NBA.com Yao Ming Info Page |publisher=NBA |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130629174229/http://www.nba.com/playerfile/yao_ming/index.html |archive-date=June 29, 2013}} Born in [[Shanghai]], Yao began playing for the Sharks as a teenager, and played on their senior team for five years in the CBA, winning a championship in his final year. After negotiating with the CBA and the Sharks to secure his release, Yao was selected by the Rockets as the [[List of first overall NBA draft picks|first overall pick]] in the [[2002 NBA draft]]. He reached the [[NBA playoffs]] four times, and in [[2009 NBA playoffs|2009]], helped the Rockets win their first playoff series since [[1997 NBA playoffs|1997]]. After missing several games due to a series of foot and ankle injuries in his last six seasons, Yao announced his retirement from professional basketball in 2011.{{Cite news |last=Passa |first=Dennis |url=https://news.yahoo.com/chinese-great-yao-ming-retires-basketball-060633532.html |title=Chinese great Yao Ming retires from basketball |agency=Associated Press |publisher=Yahoo! Sports |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111130114954/http://news.yahoo.com/chinese-great-yao-ming-retires-basketball-060633532.html |archive-date=November 30, 2011 |url-status=dead}} Among Rockets franchise leaders, Yao ranks second in total blocks, sixth in total rebounds, and ranked sixth in total points at the time of his retirement.{{cite news |title=Chinese star Houston Rockets' Yao Ming retires, ending basketball career |url=https://www.espn.com/nba/story/_/id/6785935 |publisher=ESPN |date=July 14, 2013 |access-date=July 11, 2020}} Yao is one of China's best-known athletes internationally, with sponsorships with several major companies. His rookie year in the NBA was the subject of a documentary film, ''[[The Year of the Yao]]'', and he co-wrote, along with NBA analyst [[Ric Bucher]], an autobiography titled ''Yao: A Life in Two Worlds''. Known in China as the "Yao Ming Phenomenon" and in the United States as the "Ming Dynasty", Yao's success in the NBA, and his popularity among fans, made him a symbol of a new China that was both more modern and more confident.{{Cite book |last1=Pomfret |first1=John |title=The Beautiful Country and the Middle Kingdom: American and China, 1776 to the Present |page=582 |location=New York {{convert|7|ft|3|in}}. == Professional career == === Shanghai Sharks (1997–2002) === Yao first tried out for the [[Shanghai Sharks]]' junior team of the [[Chinese Basketball Association]] (CBA) when he was 13 years old, and practiced ten hours a day for his acceptance.{{Cite book |last=Bucher |first=Ric |author2=Ming, Yao |title=Yao: A Life in Two Worlds |page=[https://archive.org/details/yao00yaom/page/31 31] |isbn=1-4013-5214-6 |url=https://archive.org/details/yao00yaom/page/31 |date=September 22, 2004 |publisher=Miamax}} After playing with the junior team for four years, Yao joined the Sharks' senior team, where he averaged 10 points and 8 [[rebound (basketball)|rebounds]] a game in his [[1997–98 Chinese Basketball Association season|rookie season]]. His next season was cut short when he broke his foot for the second time in his career, which Yao said decreased his jumping ability by four to six inches (10 to 15 cm).{{Cite book |last=Bucher |first=Ric |author2=Ming, Yao |title=Yao: A Life in Two Worlds |page=[https://archive.org/details/yao00yaom/page/50 50] |isbn=1-4013-5214-6 |url=https://archive.org/details/yao00yaom/page/50 |date=September 22, 2004 |publisher=Miamax}} The Sharks made the finals of the CBA in Yao's [[1999–2000 CBA season|third season]] and again the [[2000–01 CBA season|next year]], but lost both times to the [[Bayi Rockets]]. When [[Wang Zhizhi]] left the Bayi Rockets to become the first NBA player from China the [[2001–02 CBA season|following year]], the Sharks finally won their first CBA championship. During the playoffs in his final year with Shanghai, Yao averaged 38.9 points and 20.2 rebounds a game, while shooting 76.6% from the field,{{Cite news |url=http://www.nba.com/draft2002/profiles/yao_ming.html |title=Player Profile Yao Ming |publisher=NBA |access-date=February 9, 2009}} and made all 21 of his shots during one game in the finals.{{Cite news |last=Beech |first=Hannah |title=China's Incredible Hulk of the hard court becomes an NBA sensation |work=Time Magazine |url=http://www.time.com/time/asia/2003/heroes/yao_ming.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030422082606/http://www.time.com/time/asia/2003/heroes/yao_ming.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=April 22, 2003 |access-date=August 23, 2008 |date=April 28, 2003}} === Houston Rockets (2002–2011) === Yao was pressured to enter the [[1999 NBA draft|NBA draft in 1999]] by Li Yaomin, the deputy general manager of the Shanghai Sharks. Li also influenced Yao to sign a contract for Evergreen Sports Inc. to serve as his agent. The agreement entitled Evergreen to 33% of Yao's earnings, but the contract was later determined to be invalid.{{Cite book |last=Bucher |first=Ric |author2=Ming, Yao |title=Yao: A Life in Two Worlds |page=[https://archive.org/details/yao00yaom/page/68 68] |isbn=1-4013-5214-6 |url=https://archive.org/details/yao00yaom/page/68 |date=September 22, 2004 |publisher=Miamax}} As American attention on Yao grew, Chinese authorities also took interest. In 2002, the Chinese government released new regulations that would require him and other Chinese players to turn over half of any NBA earnings to the government and China's national basketball association, including endorsements as well as salaries.{{Cite news |last=Fackler |first=Martin |title=Beijing Could Claim Half of Chinese Star's NBA Earnings |agency=[[Associated Press]] |url=https://www.deseretnews.com/article/910072/Beijing-could-claim-half-of-Chinese-stars-NBA-earnings.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190728150150/https://www.deseretnews.com/article/910072/Beijing-could-claim-half-of-Chinese-stars-NBA-earnings.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 28, 2019 |access-date=July 29, 2019 |date=April 25, 2002}} When Yao decided to enter the [[2002 NBA draft]], a group of advisers was formed that came to be known as "Team Yao". Chinese Fans Hope Not Yet |date=July 11, 2011 |publisher=CNN |url=http://www.cnn.com/2011/SPORT/07/09/yao.ming/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110712063115/http://www.cnn.com/2011/SPORT/07/09/yao.ming/ |archive-date=July 12, 2011 |url-status=dead}}{{cite web |title=Yao tells packed press conference in Shanghai he is retiring from NBA |date=July 20, 2011 |agency=Associated Press |magazine=Sports Illustrated |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2011/basketball/nba/07/20/yao.retires.ap/index.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121104161105/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2011/basketball/nba/07/20/yao.retires.ap/index.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=November 4, 2012 |access-date=July 20, 2011}} He cited injuries to his foot and ankle, including the third fracture to his left foot sustained near the end of 2010.{{cite web |url=http://www.chron.com/disp/story.mpl/sports/bk/bkn/7660932.html |title=Rockets' Yao makes it official, retires from basketball – Houston Chronicle |publisher=Chron.com |date=July 20, 2011 |access-date=January 25, 2014}} His retirement sparked over 1.2 million comments on the Chinese social-networking site [[Sina Weibo]].{{cite web |url=http://news.xinhuanet.com/english2010/indepth/2011-07/20/c_13998245.htm |title=Yao retires, who will be the next "Chinese icon"? |publisher=News.xinhuanet.com |date=July 20, 2011 |access-date=January 25, 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131127134015/http://news.xinhuanet.com/english2010/indepth/2011-07/20/c_13998245.htm |archive-date=November 27, 2013}} Reacting to Yao's retirement, NBA commissioner [[David Stern]] said Yao was a "bridge between Chinese and American fans" and that he had "a wonderful mixture of talent, dedication, humanitarian aspirations and a sense of humor." He was also named the [[FIBA Asia Cup Most Valuable Player|MVP of all three tournaments]]. === 2006 World Championship === Yao's injury at the end of the 2005–06 NBA season required a full six months of rest, threatening his participation in the [[2006 FIBA World Championship]].{{Cite news |title=China sweats over Yao Ming's foot |publisher=redorbit.com |date=April 13, 2006 |url=http://www.redorbit.com/news/sports/468819/china_sweats_over_yao_mings_foot/ |access-date=August 23, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080430102803/http://www.redorbit.com/news/sports/468819/china_sweats_over_yao_mings_foot/ |archive-date=April 30, 2008 |url-status=dead}} However, he recovered before the start of the tournament, and in the last game of the preliminary round, he had 36 points and 10 rebounds in a win against [[Slovenia men's national basketball team|Slovenia]] to lead China into the [[Round of 16]].{{Cite news |title=Game Report, China vs Slovenia 78–77, GROUP D |publisher=FIBA.com |date=August 24, 2006 |url=http://www.fiba.com/pages/eng/fe/06_wcm/scheResu/p/eventid/3507/gamename/13/groupname/D/langid//playernumber//roundid/4742/selnodeid/627/teamnumber//zone//fe_scheStat_gameRepo.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081205164550/http://www.fiba.com/pages/eng/fe/06_wcm/scheResu/p/eventid/3507/gamename/13/groupname/D/langid/playernumber/roundid/4742/selnodeid/627/teamnumber/zone/fe_scheStat_gameRepo.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 5, 2008 |access-date=August 23, 2008}} In the first knockout round, however, China was defeated by eventual finalist [[Greece men's national basketball team|Greece]]. NBA Star Nets China's Proletarian Award |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2005-apr-28-fg-modelworker28-story.html |access-date=March 25, 2021 |work=Los Angeles Times}} == Personal life == After Yao announced that he would enter the [[2002 NBA draft]], he told one American journalist that he had been studying English for two years, and that he liked the movie ''[[Star Wars (film)|Star Wars]]'' but disliked [[hip hop]]. He was sometimes accompanied during interviews in Shanghai by one of his parents, whose basketball careers were derailed by the 1966–76 [[Cultural Revolution]], and who came to his Shanghai Sharks games on bicycles.{{Cite news |last=Fackler |first=Martin |title=Yao Ming Ready to Mix It Up with the NBA's Best |agency=[[Associated Press]] |url=https://azdailysun.com/yao-ming-ready-to-mix-it-up-with-the-nba/article_a24a905d-8a21-5523-b13f-e0adc57fbeb9.html |access-date=July 29, 2019 |date=April 27, 2002}} [[File:Yao Ming Interview.jpg|thumb|upright|Yao answers questions from reporters, October 2006]] Yao met Chinese female basketball player [[Ye Li]] when he was 17 years old. Ye was not fond of Yao at first, but finally accepted him after he gave her the team pins he had collected during the [[2000 Summer Olympics]].{{Cite news |title=Groomsman Fondly Recounts Yao Ming's Marriage |last=Zhou |first=Jing |publisher=china.org.cn |date=August 30, 2007 |url=http://www.china.org.cn/english/sports/222519.htm |access-date=March 16, 2008}} She is the only woman he has ever dated.{{Cite news |title=In Step With: Yao Ming |publisher=Parade Magazine |date=May 22, 2005 |url=http://www.parade.com/articles/editions/2005/edition_05-22-2005/in_step_with_0 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061017193757/http://www.parade.com/articles/editions/2005/edition_05-22-2005/in_step_with_0 |archive-date=October 17, 2006}} Their relationship became public when they appeared together during the 2004 Olympics closing ceremony. On August 6, 2007, Yao and Ye married in a ceremony attended by close friends and family and closed to the media.{{Cite news |title=Yao's wedding unites East and North cultures |last=Zen |first=TC Cheng |work=Houston Chronicle |date=August 7, 2007 |url=http://www.chron.com/disp/story.mpl/front/5029484.html |access-date=March 15, 2008}} On May 21, 2010, the couple's daughter Yao Qinlei ({{lang-zh|姚沁蕾}}; her English name is Amy) was born in Houston, Texas.[http://www.shanghaidaily.com/sp/article/2010/201007/20100730/article_444837.htm "Yao Ming's daughter named Amy".] ''Shanghai Daily''. July 30, 2010. Retrieved December 9, 2010.{{cite web |url=http://www.chron.com/disp/story.mpl/sports/bk/bkn/7016936.html |title=Yao's wife gives birth to seven-pound, nine-ounce baby | Chron.com – Houston Chronicle |date=May 21, 2010 |work=Houston Chronicle |access-date=May 22, 2010}} In 2004, Yao co-wrote an autobiography with [[ESPN]] sportswriter [[Ric Bucher]], entitled ''Yao: A Life in Two Worlds''.{{Cite news |last=Westbrook |first=Bruce |title=Yao's Life in Two Worlds |publisher=NBA |url=http://www.nba.com/features/yao_041001.html |access-date=April 17, 2008}} In the same year, he was also the subject of a documentary film, ''[[The Year of the Yao]]'', which focuses on his NBA rookie year.{{Cite news |last=Westbrook |first=Bruce |title=The Year of the Yao |work=Houston Chronicle |url=http://www.chron.com/disp/story.mpl/ae/movies/reviews/3134692.html |access-date=March 16, 2008}} The film is narrated by his friend and interpreter, Colin Pine.{{Cite news |last=Lacy |first=Liam |title=The Year of the Yao |publisher=The Globe and Mail |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/arts/the-year-of-the-yao/article20421929/ |date=May 5, 2005 |access-date=August 5, 2018 |language=en}} In 2005, former ''[[Newsweek]]'' writer Brook Larmer published a book entitled ''Operation Yao Ming'', in which he said that Yao's parents were convinced to marry each other so that they would produce a dominant athlete, and that during Yao's childhood, he was given special treatment to help him become a great basketball player. In a 2015 AMA post on [[Reddit]], Yao stated that this was not true and that he started playing basketball for fun at age 9.{{cite web |url=https://www.reddit.com/r/IAmA/comments/2m7f9u/i_am_yao_ming_wildlife_advocate_ama/cm1li12 |title=I am Yao Ming, wildlife advocate. AMA.; Reddit.com |date=November 13, 2014}} In 2009, Yao provided the voice for a character of a Chinese animated film, ''[[The Magic Aster]]'', released on June 19.{{cite news |title=Yao Ming voices role in Chinese animated film |agency=Associated Press |date=June 5, 2009 |url=https://www.google.com/hostednews/ap/article/ALeqM5j93yJ7P3uihf1FK3Wpla69MtlgLgD98KBC7G0 |access-date=June 5, 2009}}{{dead link|date=June 2024|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}} Yao enrolled at the Antai College of Economics & Management of [[Shanghai Jiao Tong University]] in 2011.{{cite news |title=Chinese Yao and his wife, Ye Li, are the godparents of the cruise ship [[Majestic Princess]] of [[Princess Cruises]], christening the ship on July 9, 2017.{{Cite web|url=http://mobile.ytsports.cn/news-3473.html|title=Yao Ming christens Majestic Princess|website=mobile.Ytsports.cn|access-date=June 6, 2026}} ==Other activities== ===Commercial engagements=== [[File:Secretary Kerry Chats With Former NBA Player Yao After Wildlife Trafficking Event in Beijing (14611584355) (cropped).jpg|thumb|right|Yao (left) with [[United States Secretary of State]] [[John Kerry]] at the [[U.S.–China Strategic and Economic Dialogue]] in 2014]] Yao is one of China's most recognizable athletes.{{Cite news |last=Patrick |first=Dick |title=Yao Ming's Injury Could Send Reebok Reeling |work=USA Today |date=May 24, 2006 |url=https://www.usatoday.com/sports/olympics/summer/track/2006-05-24-beijing-hurdles_x.htm |access-date=March 20, 2008}} As of 2009, he had led [[Forbes]]' [[China Celebrity 100|Chinese celebrities list]] in income and popularity for six straight years, earning US$51 million ([[CN¥]]357 million) in 2008.{{Cite news |url=http://www.chinadaily.com.cn/showbiz/2009-03/18/content_7591787.htm |title=Yao tops forbes list again, but Ziyi catches up |date=March 18, 2009 |work=China Daily |access-date=March 28, 2009}} A major part of his income comes from his sponsorship deals,{{Cite news |last=Pells |first=Eddie |work=Houston Chronicle |title=Injury doesn't diminish Yao's ability to sell products |date=March 11, 2008 |url=http://www.chron.com/disp/story.mpl/sports/5610303.html |access-date=March 16, 2008}} as he is under contract with several major companies to endorse their products. He was signed by [[Nike, Inc.|Nike]] until the end of his rookie season. When Nike decided not to renew his contract, he signed with [[Reebok]].{{Cite news |last=Rovell |first=Darren |title=Yao Ming's Injury Could Send Reebok Reeling |publisher=[[CNBC]] |date=September 14, 2007 |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2008/02/27/yao-mings-injury-could-send-reebok-reeling.html?__source=RSS*blog*&par=RSS |access-date=March 16, 2008}} He also had a deal with [[Pepsi]], and he successfully sued [[The Coca-Cola Company|Coca-Cola]] in 2003 when they used his image on their bottles while promoting the national team.{{Cite news |title=Yao Ming, Coke's China subsidiary settle lawsuit |publisher=ESPN |date=October 17, 2003 |url=https://www.espn.com/espn/wire?id=1640181 |access-date=July 11, 2020}} He eventually signed with Coca-Cola for the 2008 Olympics. |url=http://www.nba.com/bwb/asia2005_report.html |access-date=March 16, 2008}} In the NBA's offseason in 2003, Yao hosted a telethon, which raised US$300,000 to help stop the spread of [[Severe acute respiratory syndrome|SARS]].{{Cite news |title=Yao implores everyone to join in battling SARS |publisher=ESPN |date=May 8, 2003 |url=https://assets.espn.go.com/nba/news/2003/0508/1550841.html match to raise money for underprivileged children in China. He was joined by fellow NBA stars [[Steve Nash]], [[Carmelo Anthony]], and [[Baron Davis]], and Hong Kong actor [[Jackie Chan]].{{Cite news |title=Yao scores 21 points in charity game |publisher=Xinhau |date=September 14, 2007 |url=http://news.xinhuanet.com/english/2007-09/15/content_6724598.htm |access-date=March 16, 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080601225634/http://news.xinhuanet.com/english/2007-09/15/content_6724598.htm |archive-date=June 1, 2008 |df=mdy-all}} After the [[2008 Sichuan earthquake]], Yao donated $2 million to relief work and created the Yao Ming Foundation to help rebuild schools destroyed in the earthquake.{{Cite news |url=https://www.nba.com/rockets/news/yao_foundation_080610.html |title=Yao Ming Announces Launch of Foundation |date=June 10, 2008 |publisher=NBA |access-date=May 13, 2009}}{{Cite web |url=http://www.theyaomingfoundation.org/index.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100112164130/http://www.theyaomingfoundation.org/index.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 12, 2010 |title=The Yao Ming Foundation |website=Theyaomingfoundation.org |access-date=February 9, 2018 }} ===Conservation work=== [[File:Yao Ming in Beijing in 2016 (cropped).jpg|thumb|Yao in Beijing in 2016]] Yao partnered with [[WildAid]] to appear in commercials and documentaries to educate citizens on the harmful effects of [[shark fin soup]] on shark species. From 2011 to 2018, consumption of shark fin soup dropped by 70% in China.{{Cite web |last=Musaddique |first=Shafi |title=Yao Ming: NBA legend builds schools, fights shark fin soup in China |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2018/07/16/yao-ming-nba-legend-builds-schools-fights-shark-fin-soup-in-china.html |access-date=2023-04-06 |website=CNBC |date=July 20, 2018 |language=en}} In August 2012, Yao started filming a documentary about the [[northern white rhinoceros]].{{cite web |author=Rhishja Cota-Larson |url=https://planetsave.com/2012/08/17/rhino-crisis-round-up-yao-ming-in-kenya-more/ |title=Rhino Crisis Round Up: Yao Ming in Kenya & More |publisher=PlanetSave |date=August 17, 2012 |access-date=January 25, 2014}} He is also an ambassador for [[Elephant#Conservation|elephant conservation]].{{cite news |url=https://www.economist.com/news/middle-east-and-africa/21565651-conservationists-use-new-tactics-battle-poachers-brought-tusk |newspaper=The Economist |title=Brought to tusk |date=November 3, 2012}} In 2014, he was also part of the documentary ''[[The End of the Wild]]'' about elephant conservation. Yao has filmed a number of public service announcements for elephant and rhino conservation for the "Say No" campaign with partners African Wildlife Foundation and WildAid.{{cite web |url=https://www.awf.org/projects/say-no-campaign |title=Say No Campaign |date=June 30, 2014 |publisher=African Wildlife Foundation |access-date=June 30, 2014}} ===Politics=== On March 3, 2013, Yao attended the First Session of the [[Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference|12th Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference]] as one of its 2,200 members.{{Cite web |date=3 March 2013 |title=Yao Ming a focus at CPPCC venue |url=http://www.china.org.cn/china/NPC_CPPCC_2013/2013-03/03/content_28113072_3.htm |access-date=2021-03-25 |website=China.org.cn}} He was a member of the CPPCC from 2013 to 2018.
